16.1 Example 1: average car mileage by postcode area
These examples use only the aggregate tables and a spreadsheet. The steps are written for Excel; other spreadsheets work the same way. The results shown were calculated from the same files, so you can check your answer against them.
Question: How far is the average car driven in each postcode area, and which areas have the highest and lowest mileage?
File: tables/mileage/mileage_by_pca_year_body_fuel.csv
Steps:
Result: the national average is 6,620 miles per car.
Interpreting it: low averages in London, and high ones in more rural areas, are what you would expect. section: 16.3 Example 3: the fleet by Euro standard
text:
16.3 Example 3: the fleet by Euro standard
Question: How has the share of cars meeting each Euro standard changed?
File: tables/profile/a1_counts_cars.csv. This is a wide table: one row per year, and one column for each category of each characteristic, named characteristic: category.
Steps:

Open the file. Hide or delete the columns you don’t need, keeping year and the euro_standard: ... columns.
Add a column adding up the Euro standard columns for each year, and divide each column by it to get shares.
Select the year column and the share columns, and insert a line chart.









Figure 16.1: Share of cars by Euro standard, among cars with a plausible mileage in Great Britain. Most Euro standards are assumed from the date of manufacture (Chapter 4).





Interpreting it: the chart shows each standard rising as new cars meet it and falling as those cars age and leave the fleet. The profile tables count only cars with a plausible mileage that year, and exclude Northern Ireland.






ImportantSpotting a problem: Euro 6 cars in 2005



The chart shows 4.5% of cars as Euro 6 in 2005, nearly ten years before the standard existed. These are not real. They are cars whose Euro status was missing and was filled from similar vehicles (the same make, model, birth year and fuel), where a single wrong value recorded for one vehicle was copied to the rest of its group. The vehicle table flags them with euro_check = 'later_than_date'.
This is a good example of why you should check where values come from before relying on them. Most Euro standards in the data are filled or assumed rather than recorded; the euro_source: ... columns of the same table show how many of each. For a defensible analysis of Euro standards, use the vehicle table and exclude or correct values flagged later_than_date (Chapter 14, pitfall 7).

title: 17  Worked examples: code
text:
-- Vehicles observed in 2022, by body type and fuel group.
-- "Observed" means the vehicle has a real postcode area in 2022,
-- not one of the statuses unborn, dead or unknown.
SELECT
  body_type,
  fuel_simple,
  count(*) AS n_vehicles
FROM read_parquet('vehicles_enhanced.parquet')
WHERE pca_2022 NOT IN ('unborn', 'dead', 'unknown')
GROUP BY body_type, fuel_simple
ORDER BY n_vehicles DESC;

title: 17  Worked examples: code
section: 17.2 Example 2: reshaping to one row per vehicle per year
text:
17.2 Example 2: reshaping to one row per vehicle per year
Question: How does the annual mileage of a Ford Fiesta change as it ages, and has that changed over time?
The vehicle table has one column per year. To analyse by age, the year columns need to become rows. DuckDB’s UNPIVOT does this: the mileage and plausibility columns are unpivoted separately and joined back together by vehicle and year. Filtering to one model first keeps the reshaped table small.
-- Average annual mileage of Ford Fiestas by age, for three years.
-- The vehicle table is wide (one column per year), so the mileage and
-- plausibility columns are first turned into long form: one row per
-- vehicle per year.
WITH fiesta AS (
  SELECT *
  FROM read_parquet('vehicles_enhanced.parquet')
  WHERE make_final = 'FORD' AND model_final = 'FIESTA'
),
mileage AS (
  UNPIVOT (SELECT vehicle_id, COLUMNS('^mileage_[0-9]{4}$') FROM fiesta)
  ON COLUMNS('^mileage_') INTO NAME col VALUE mileage
),
legit AS (
  UNPIVOT (SELECT vehicle_id, COLUMNS('^legit_mileage_[0-9]{4}$') FROM fiesta)
  ON COLUMNS('^legit_mileage_') INTO NAME col VALUE legit
)
SELECT
  CAST(right(m.col, 4) AS INTEGER) AS year,
  CAST(right(m.col, 4) AS INTEGER) - year(f.first_use_date) AS age,
  count(*) AS n_vehicles,
  round(avg(m.mileage)) AS mean_mileage,
  median(m.mileage) AS median_mileage
FROM mileage m
JOIN legit l
  ON l.vehicle_id = m.vehicle_id AND right(l.col, 4) = right(m.col, 4)
JOIN fiesta f ON f.vehicle_id = m.vehicle_id
WHERE l.legit                          -- plausible mileage only
  AND right(m.col, 4) IN ('2010', '2016', '2022')
GROUP BY year, age
HAVING age BETWEEN 3 AND 20
ORDER BY year, age;








Figure 17.1: Average annual mileage of Ford Fiestas by age, plausible mileage only.





Mileage falls with age, and the whole curve is lower in 2022 than in 2010. The query starts at age 3. A Fiesta has no odometer reading before its first MOT at three, so its mileage in earlier years can only come from sharing out the distance since new, and says little about use at each age.

text:
17.3 Example 3: recorded against filled values
Question: Does the CO2 of new petrol and diesel cars depend on whether the value was recorded or filled from similar vehicles?
co2_src records where each harmonised value came from. Comparing the average of all values with the average of recorded values only is a quick test of whether filling gaps has changed a result.
-- CO2 of petrol and diesel cars first used 2012-2019: all values against
-- recorded values only. co2_src says where each value came from.
SELECT
  year(first_use_date) AS first_use_year,
  fuel_simple,
  count(co2) AS n_with_co2,
  round(avg(co2), 1) AS mean_co2_all,
  count(co2) FILTER (WHERE co2_src = 'dvla') AS n_recorded,
  round(avg(co2) FILTER (WHERE co2_src = 'dvla'), 1) AS mean_co2_recorded
FROM read_parquet('vehicles_enhanced.parquet')
WHERE body_type = 'Cars'
  AND fuel_simple IN ('Petrol', 'Diesel')
  AND year(first_use_date) BETWEEN 2012 AND 2019
GROUP BY first_use_year, fuel_simple
ORDER BY fuel_simple, first_use_year;

title: 17  Worked examples: code
text:
17.4 Example 4: following a cohort
Question: What happened to the cars first used in 2008?
-- What happened to the cars first used in 2008? For each year, count how
-- many were observed, unknown or dead. Only the pca_YYYY columns are needed.
WITH cohort AS (
  SELECT vehicle_id, COLUMNS('^pca_[0-9]{4}$')
  FROM read_parquet('vehicles_enhanced.parquet')
  WHERE body_type = 'Cars' AND year(first_use_date) = 2008
),
long AS (
  UNPIVOT cohort ON COLUMNS('^pca_') INTO NAME col VALUE pca
)
SELECT
  CAST(right(col, 4) AS INTEGER) AS year,
  CASE WHEN pca IN ('unborn', 'dead', 'unknown') THEN pca
       ELSE 'observed' END AS status,
  count(*) AS n_vehicles
FROM long
GROUP BY year, status
ORDER BY year, status;








Figure 17.2: Cars first used in 2008, by their status in each year.





Almost the whole cohort is observed from 2008, although most cars had their first MOT only in 2011: once a car has been tested, its first postcode area is copied back to its first registration (Chapter 6). The cohort then gradually becomes dead as cars stop being tested, about two years after their last MOT, because the postcode area is carried forward. The few cars observed before 2008 have a first-use date later than their first record, such as imports or re-registered vehicles. The unknown line rises again at the end of the series: cars that may simply not have been tested yet (Chapter 14, pitfall 4).

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
Annualisation

Converting each vehicle’s test history into one figure per calendar year (Chapter 8).

Backfill

Filling a missing attribute with the most common value among similar vehicles: the same make, model, birth year and fuel (Chapter 9).

Birth date

In CARS, the earliest of a vehicle’s first-use, registration and manufacture dates.

Body type

DfT’s classification of vehicles into cars, light goods vehicles, motorcycles, buses and coaches, heavy goods vehicles and other vehicles (Chapter 3).

CAZ

Clean Air Zone: an area in which the most polluting vehicles are charged or restricted (Chapter 4).

Churn

The change in the vehicles in an area from year to year as vehicles arrive, move and leave.

DfT

Department for Transport.

DVA

Driver & Vehicle Agency, Northern Ireland.

DVLA

Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency, which keeps the vehicle register.

DVSA

Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency, which runs the MOT scheme.

Euro standard

A European limit on the air pollutants a new vehicle may emit (Chapter 4).

First-use date

The date a vehicle was first used on the road, normally its first registration.

Generic model

DfT’s grouping of model variants under one name, such as FORD FIESTA.

HGV

Heavy goods vehicle: a goods vehicle over 3.5 tonnes.

LGV

Light goods vehicle: a goods vehicle up to 3.5 tonnes; a van or pick-up.

MAUP

Modifiable areal unit problem: results from area data depend on the size and shape of the areas (Chapter 7).

MOT test

The annual roadworthiness test for vehicles three years old and over (Chapter 1).

Observed

In CARS, a vehicle is observed in a year when it has a postcode area in that year.

OGL

Open Government Licence.

Parquet

A compressed, column-based file format for large tables.

PCA

Postcode area: the one or two letters at the start of a postcode (Chapter 7).

PHEV

Plug-in hybrid electric vehicle.

Plausible mileage

An annual mileage the Bristol annualisation judged believable (legit_mileage_YYYY = TRUE).

SORN

Statutory Off Road Notification: a declaration that a vehicle is kept off the road (Chapter 6).

Test class

The class of MOT test a vehicle takes (Chapter 3).

Type approval

Certification that a vehicle design meets the rules for its category (M1, N1 and so on) (Chapter 3).

V5C

The vehicle registration certificate, or logbook.

VES

The DVLA’s Vehicle Enquiry Service.

VRM

Vehicle registration mark: the registration number (Chapter 5).

WLTP, NEDC

The laboratory tests used to measure official fuel consumption and CO2; WLTP replaced NEDC in 2017–2018.

title: Appendix D — Maintaining this book
section: D.2 How data gets into the book
text:
D.2 How data gets into the book
Nothing in the book reads the pipeline repository directly. Instead:

data/manifest.yml lists every file the book uses from MOT-pipline.
scripts/sync-pipeline.R copies those files into data/pipeline/ (data) and reports/ (the pipeline’s reports, shown as appendices), and records the pipeline’s commit in data/pipeline/provenance.csv.
scripts/run-examples.R runs each query in sql/ against the vehicle table and saves the result in data/examples/. The worked examples display the same .sql files, so the code shown is exactly the code that produced the results.
Chapters read the copies with read_pipeline() and read_example() from R/book.R, and compute every number, table and chart from them when the book is rendered.

The copies are committed, so anyone can rebuild the book without access to the pipeline or the 9 GB vehicle table.

title: Appendix D — Maintaining this book
section: D.3 Updating after a new pipeline build
text:
D.3 Updating after a new pipeline build
From the book’s root folder, with MOT-pipline checked out alongside it (or MOT_PIPELINE_DIR set to its location):
Rscript scripts/sync-pipeline.R   # copy the new outputs
Rscript scripts/run-examples.R    # rerun the examples (needs the parquet)
Rscript scripts/rebuild.R         # re-execute every chapter and render
Then check the result, and commit data/, reports/ and _freeze/. Pushing to main publishes the book.






ImportantCheck the words, not just the numbers



Numbers in the text are computed, but sentences that interpret them (“the two averages are almost identical”, “most were still tested in Leeds”) are written by hand. After a rebuild, read the chapters whose figures changed and make sure the text still fits.


If a pipeline file used by the book is renamed or removed, the sync script stops with an error naming it. Update data/manifest.yml and the chapter that reads it.

title: Appendix D — Maintaining this book
section: D.4 Why rebuild.R clears the frozen results
text:
D.4 Why rebuild.R clears the frozen results
The book uses Quarto’s freeze option: the results of each chapter’s code are stored in _freeze/ and reused until that chapter’s source changes. This is what lets GitHub Actions publish the book without R. It also means a plain quarto render will not pick up new data, because the chapters themselves have not changed. scripts/rebuild.R deletes _freeze/ so that every chapter runs again.

title: Appendix D — Maintaining this book
section: D.5 Adding pipeline data to a chapter
text:
D.5 Adding pipeline data to a chapter

Add the file to data/manifest.yml.
Run Rscript scripts/sync-pipeline.R.
In the chapter, source("R/book.R") and read it with read_pipeline("outputs", "tables", ...).

To add a worked example, put the query in sql/ (naming the file as 'vehicles_enhanced.parquet'), run Rscript scripts/run-examples.R exNN, and show it with {{< include ../sql/exNN_name.sql >}} inside a sql code block.

title: Appendix D — Maintaining this book
text:
D.6 Writing conventions

Placeholders for material still to come are callouts titled To be written (or To be confirmed for statements to check), with the class .todo. Search the chapters for .todo to list them.
Pitfalls are callouts titled Pitfall: …, and each is also summarised in



Charts use theme_cars() and the palette in R/book.R, with at most four series each.

title: Appendix D — Maintaining this book
text:
D.7 Publishing
.github/workflows/publish.yml renders the book from the frozen results and publishes it to the gh-pages branch on every push to main. One-off set-up: run quarto publish gh-pages once locally to create the branch, then in the repository’s settings set GitHub Pages to deploy from the gh-pages branch. The book will then be at cars-project.github.io/documentation.
To preview locally, run quarto preview.

title: Methodology
text:
Contents
Generated from reports/methodology.qmd by the MOT-pipline methodology_doc target. Every figure comes from the latest build (profile: main). Edit the template, not this file.
This document describes how MOT-pipline turns the Bristol vehicle-level MOT table into the enhanced vehicle dataset and summary tables. For each stage it sets out what is done, how, and the assumptions behind it, so users of the outputs can judge how far to rely on each column.
The code for each stage is named in its section. Column-level definitions are in outputs/data_dictionary.csv, which the pipeline writes.

title: Methodology
text:
1. Overview
flowchart TD
    A[Bristol annualised table<br/>138.2M rows] --> B[Stage 1: Core table<br/>scope, dates, PCA status]
    A --> M[Stage 3a: DVSA-DVLA record match<br/>make aliases, mismatch list]
    B --> C[Stage 2: Make / model<br/>DfT naming]
    T[DfT VEH0220 / VEH0124] --> C
    B --> F[Stage 3b: Fuel and engine references]
    C --> F
    M --> F
    F --> D[Stage 3c: Backfill reference tables]
    B --> E[Stage 4: Enhanced vehicle table]
    C --> E
    D --> E
    F --> E
    E --> G[Stage 5: Churn tables]
    E --> L[Life path charts<br/>one per postcode area]
    E --> H[Stage 6: Mileage summaries]
    E --> I[Stage 7: Data quality report and documents]
All processing of the full table happens in DuckDB (SQL over parquet files). Only small tables come back into R: distinct make/model pairs, make aliases and aggregated results. The pipeline is managed by R targets, which rebuilds only the stages affected by a change.
Principles applied throughout:

Supplied values are never overwritten. Cleaned, harmonised or backfilled values go into new columns next to the originals.
Every inferred value records its source. Examples are first_use_source, make_method, model_method, *_src, the scope_* flags, dvla_match, fuel_check and engine_check.
Weak evidence is flagged, not acted on. A value is only changed when the vehicle’s own records disagree and a second source settles it.
Results are deterministic. Ties are broken by explicit rules, and random sampling (sample project only) uses a fixed seed.

title: Methodology
text:
2. Input data
Source: annualised_with_ves_4.parquet, produced by the Bristol team and accessed through the RDSF.



Property
Value




Rows
138,238,617


Distinct DVSA registrations
138,238,617


Columns
202


Years covered
2005–2025 (2025 is a partial year)



The January 2026 delivery (jan26_annualised_with_2025_anon_and_ves.parquet) differed from the earlier annualised_with_ves.parquet in three ways. It added 2025. It had 5,997 fewer rows, exactly the number of surplus duplicate registrations in the earlier file, so the duplicates were removed. And it renamed every VES column to carry a _DVLA suffix, while replacing the lookup bookkeeping columns (n_api_vehicles_with_vrm, vrm_in_ves, n_ves_obs) with a fuller set that counts the lookups and records what changed between them. The pipeline reads either layout: see resolve_core_columns() in R/stage_core.R.
The file has one row per vehicle, with:

Vehicle attributes from the DVSA MOT history API: make, model, fuel, engine size, colours, first used / registration / manufacture dates, and the anonymised test class (test_class_ANON).
Per-year columns for each year 2005–2025:

mileage_YYYY: annual mileage
pca_YYYY: postcode area
legit_mileage_YYYY: whether the mileage is plausible
is_new_vehicle_YYYY, is_intertest_YYYY, is_end_use_YYYY: status flags

DVLA Vehicle Enquiry Service (VES) columns: make, fuel, engine capacity, weight, CO2, Euro status, type approval, wheel plan, tax and MOT status, and key dates. These are attached by registration.
VES lookup bookkeeping: how often VES was queried for the registration (n_VES_checks, renamed n_VES_checks_to_linked_DVSA_regs in the October 2026 ves_4 delivery, which also counts the checks against the DVLA registration alone in n_VES_checks_for_DVLA_reg; both include errored checks), how often it answered (n_VES_returns), the first and last of each, whether the last lookup errored (is_error, error), and flags for what changed between lookups: plate_ever_changed_VES, ever_SORN, v5C_issue_date_ever_changed, change_in_other_VES_field and ever_export_marked (a count, not a flag).

Assumptions about the input:

Bristol’s annualisation is taken as given. The pipeline does not re-derive annual mileage, postcode area or the per-year flags; see Bristol’s documentation for how they are built. In particular, the mileage columns are treated as annual miles (mean 7,065 in 2018) and are not rescaled.
The VES record is not always the same vehicle. Because VES is attached by registration, a registration that has moved to another vehicle brings that vehicle’s record. Section 5.1 detects these.
Gaps are common.

test_class_ANON is missing for 64.2M rows.
firstUsedDate_DVSA is missing for 61.4M rows.
VES columns are missing wherever no VES record was found (23.9% of rows).

title: Methodology
text:
3. Stage 1: Core vehicle table
Code: R/stage_core.R · Output: outputs/intermediate/01_core.parquet

3.1 Identifiers and duplicates

vehicle_id is the row number in the input file. It is stable only for that input file; a new Bristol delivery will renumber vehicles.
dup_vrm is TRUE when the DVSA registration appears on more than one row. No registration appears more than once in this input (earlier deliveries had duplicates). Duplicates are kept and flagged, not removed, because it is not known which row is correct.



3.2 Dates

birth_date is the earliest of DVSA first used date, registration date and manufacture date. Only 10,030 input vehicles have none of these.
first_use_date is the first available of:

DVSA first used date
DVLA month of first registration
birth_date

first_use_source records which one was used.
last_mot_year is the latest year with is_end_use_YYYY = TRUE. Where no year is flagged, it is the last year with a recorded postcode area, unless that year is one of the final two years of data.

Why the fallback: the January 2026 Bristol delivery leaves the end-of-use flag off for most vehicles that stopped being tested. For example, 1.6 million of the 2.4 million vehicles whose last MOT was in 2019 have no flag, against 20 thousand in the earlier delivery. Without the fallback, those vehicles would be unknown for ever, not dead. Where a vehicle has both a flag and a recorded postcode area, the flag year is its last postcode area year for 99.9% of vehicles. A vehicle last seen in the final two years may simply not be due a test yet, so it keeps no last MOT year and stays unknown.
Assumptions:

Birth date is the earliest recorded date. For vehicles that sat in stock, or were imported, the manufacture date can be well before first use.
The DVLA month of first registration is the first of that month, so it is accurate to the month only.
Vehicles with no dates get no invented one. The previous code assigned 2000-01-01 to such vehicles; that placeholder has been removed.



3.3 Postcode area status infill
Bristol’s pca_YYYY is blank in any year where the vehicle was not observed. Each blank is replaced with a status:



Condition (checked in order)
pca_YYYY becomes




A postcode area is recorded
the postcode area, unchanged


Birth year is the same as or later than year YYYY
unborn


The last MOT year (last_mot_year) is earlier than YYYY
dead


Otherwise
unknown



Assumptions:

“Dead” means no longer observed, not scrapped. A vehicle is dead in every year after the year of its last MOT. This includes vehicles that were exported, declared off-road (SORN), or simply stopped being tested.
Unobserved years before the last MOT are “unknown”. For example, a new car in its first three years before its first MOT is unknown rather than dead. This prevents vehicles from apparently coming back to life when their first MOT appears.
Birth is compared by calendar year. A vehicle born during 2010 with no recorded PCA in 2010 is unborn for 2010.
A vehicle with no dates is treated as already born in every year. It is then dead or unknown by the rules above.
Recorded postcode areas are used as supplied, including single-letter areas (B, G, L, …). The data covers the whole UK: Northern Ireland is coded NI rather than its postcode area BT (which does not occur), and a small number of vehicles have the code XX, left as supplied.



3.4 Scope: which vehicles are kept
The output aims to include every vehicle that existed at some point from 2005 onwards, including vehicles that are too new to have been tested and vehicles that were never tested. A vehicle is kept if any of these is true (scope start date 2005-01-01, set in config.yml):








Flag
Rule
Input vehicles meeting it




scope_mileage
Total mileage across all years > 0
77,265,716


scope_pca
A postcode area recorded in any year
75,437,173


scope_born
birth_date on or after the start date
59,048,329


scope_dvla_activity
DVLA tax due, last V5C issue, MOT expiry or first registration date on or after the start date
71,810,699



Vehicles kept under each rule:



Rule
Vehicles kept




Previous code: mileage OR born since 2005
89,014,223


This pipeline: any of the four flags
93,352,241



Assumptions:

A DVLA record dated 2005 or later is evidence the vehicle existed then. Examples are a V5C issued or tax due in that period.
Vehicles with none of these signals are assumed to have left the fleet before 2005. This includes every vehicle with no dates at all.
Total mileage is a plain sum across years, so a small negative value can offset a positive one. This is rare.



3.5 Tidying

VES columns get a _DVLA suffix where the delivery does not already use one (in earlier files make becomes make_DVLA; the January 2026 file supplies make_DVLA already). The VES lookup bookkeeping columns are carried through under their own names, whichever set the delivery has.
engineSize_DVSA is converted to an integer; non-numeric values become missing.
The last MOT test date is taken from final_test_date_DVSA and published under that name. DVSA now put a date in the future in lastMotTestDate_DVSA for the untested vehicles DVLA supplies (5.22M of them in the October 2026 file, the latest 2028-12-30); final_test_date_DVSA equals it on every tested vehicle and is missing rather than invented on the rest. A delivery that has only lastMotTestDate_DVSA falls back to it, converted from text to a date.
The is_new_vehicle, is_intertest and is_end_use flags are dropped after use. legit_mileage_YYYY is kept for the mileage summaries.

title: Methodology
text:
4. Stage 2: Make and model
Code: R/make_model.R · Outputs: outputs/intermediate/dft_*.parquet, outputs/intermediate/make_model_*.parquet, outputs/quality/make_model_review.csv
Makes and models follow the naming of the DfT vehicle licensing statistics: tables VEH0220 (vehicles by make, generic model, model, fuel and engine size) and VEH0124 (by make, generic model, model and year of first use), which DfT builds from the DVLA register. Using the same names means MOT results can be joined to, and checked against, the official counts. No language model is used: every step is a rule, and every result records how it was reached.







Column
Meaning




make_final
DfT make, upper case (FORD, MERCEDES)


model_final
DfT generic model without the make (FIESTA, C CLASS, 1 SERIES)


dft_genmodel
The DfT GenModel (FORD FIESTA), for joins to DfT tables


dft_model
The DfT model string, when the raw model is exactly one


derivative_final
The rest of the raw model text: trim, engine, body style


body_type
DfT body type (Cars, Light goods vehicles, Motorcycles, …)


make_method, model_method, model_confidence, body_type_src
How each was found



Of 93,352,241 in-scope vehicles, 94.9% have a DfT generic model, 4.3% have a placeholder model such as UNKNOWN (so no model), and 0.8% keep their normalised raw model because nothing matched.

4.1 The DfT reference
inputs/df_VEH0220.csv and inputs/df_VEH0124_AM.csv / _NZ.csv are read as Latin-1 text. Each count is the number of vehicles (licensed plus SORN) at the end of a year, from 2014. To name models, each row is weighted by its largest count in any year, so a model that has since left the fleet still counts.
DfT’s coding has some quirks, which are tidied before matching:

Makes spelt two ways are merged. Makes differing only in punctuation or spaces (IVECO-FORD / IVECO FORD) join the larger. inputs/make_aliases.csv merges others: DfT files most Mercedes-Benz vehicles under MERCEDES, and uses MERCEDES-BENZ for recent registrations whose generic model is just the model text.
Generic models that are just a model string are recoded. Some recent registrations have a GenModel of the make plus the model string (HYUNDAI TUCSON ADVANCE PHEV AUTO). These model strings are matched like raw text against the rest of the make (TUCSON).
A long generic model name that extends a much more common one joins it, when it adds two or more words and has a tenth of the vehicles or fewer.
MODEL MISSING is no model.

Four reference tables come out of this (outputs/intermediate/dft_*.parquet): model names and body types, fuel group by engine band (used to settle ambiguous models, Section 4.4), year of first use, and the fuel as DfT records it, which is the only source that separates plug-in hybrids from other hybrids and is used in Section 5.5.


4.2 Makes
Each distinct raw make is resolved once. The first step that matches wins:

Text that starts with the make’s name (MINI COOPER) is also tried without it. Matches from the prefix, words and fuzzy steps must fit the vehicles’ MOT test class: motorcycles (classes 1 and 2) need a generic model that DfT mostly records as motorcycles, and other classes one it mostly does not. This stops HONDA S-WING 125 becoming the S800 car.
model_confidence is the share of the DfT vehicles under the matched text that have the chosen generic model: 1 for exact and generic, at least 0.9 for prefix and words.


4.4 Choices made per vehicle
For ambiguous and make_only text, each candidate generic model starts from its share of the DfT vehicles under the text. That share is multiplied by how common the vehicle’s fuel group and engine size band, and its year of first use, are among DfT vehicles of that generic model (with add-half smoothing, so a combination DfT never records is unlikely but possible). The candidate with the largest weight is chosen, and model_confidence is its share of the total weight. 936,073 vehicles are chosen this way, and 129,941 vehicles have a model_confidence below 0.5.
Engine size bands follow DfT: up to 50cc, 51–125cc, 126–200cc, then 100cc steps. Fuel groups are petrol, diesel, electric, hybrid (including plug-in and range extended), gas and other.


4.5 Derivative
derivative_final is the raw model text after the words that gave the make and model, kept as recorded apart from case and spacing. FIESTA ZETEC CLIMATE gives ZETEC CLIMATE; 118I M SPORT keeps all its words, because the badge is not part of the generic model name 1 SERIES. It is not standardised: it keeps the detail the DfT scheme drops (Discovery SPORT, C4 GRAND PICASSO) for analyses that need it. A derivative that only repeats the start of the model name (E for E CLASS) is dropped.


4.6 Body type
body_type uses the DfT body types. The first source that gives one wins (body_type_src):

4.7 Reviewed decisions and the review list

inputs/make_model_overrides.csv is applied last and wins over every step. Each row fixes one raw make/model spelling, gives the DfT make, generic model and derivative, and states the evidence. It is checked when read: a make is required, each raw pair may appear once, every row needs a reason, and a model must be a DfT generic model of the make. It has 15 rows. The first came from the fuel checks in Section 5.3, which caught an earlier lookup giving electric models to old petrol vehicles (PORSCHE TARGA as a Taycan).
inputs/make_aliases.csv merges make spellings (Sections 4.1 and 4.2), with a reason for each.
outputs/quality/make_model_review.csv lists the raw pairs most worth reviewing, by vehicles: those matched by spelling fixes, word sets or vehicle attributes, or not matched at all, with the three nearest generic models of the make. Adding reviewed rows to the overrides file is how the matching improves.

Edit these files in R or a text editor. A spreadsheet re-saves numbers in its own format (45.160 becomes 45.16, 130E18 becomes 1.3E+020), which changes the raw keys.

R/dft_compare.R counts the in-scope vehicles observed in each year (a real PCA, not unborn, dead or unknown) by body type, age and make/model, and sets them against VEH0124’s licensed plus SORN counts (outputs/quality/dft_stock_*.csv). unknown is left out because it never ends for a vehicle with no last MOT year. Both sources cover the whole UK, Northern Ireland included. They differ by design: vehicles under three years old (four in Northern Ireland) have no MOT, and a SORN vehicle stays in DfT’s count but is not tested. title: Methodology
section: 5. Stage 3: Record matching, fuel and engine checks, and backfill
text:
5. Stage 3: Record matching, fuel and engine checks, and backfill
Code: R/dvla_match.R, R/fuel_engine.R, R/euro_status.R, R/backfill.R (reference tables) and R/assemble.R (application) · Outputs: outputs/quality/dvla_make_aliases.csv, outputs/quality/suspected_dvla_mismatches.csv, outputs/intermediate/fuel_*.parquet, outputs/intermediate/backfill_*.parquet, then columns in the enhanced table
Eight attributes are harmonised: fuel, engine_cc, revenue_weight, co2, euro_status, type_approval, wheelplan and test_class. The stage runs in four steps:

Check whether each VES record describes the same vehicle (5.1).
Decide the fuel from the vehicle’s own records, then check it against its make/model (5.2, 5.3).
Set the engine size, with 0 for vehicles that have no engine (5.4).
Fill remaining gaps from vehicles with the same fuel (5.5, 5.6).

Figures below are for the 93,352,241 in-scope vehicles.

5.1 DVSA–DVLA record match
The DVSA and VES records of each vehicle are compared in three independent ways:







Comparison
Disagrees when




Make
The makes differ after removing punctuation, neither is a prefix of the other, and they do not share their first five characters. Known naming pairs (below) agree.


Year
Manufacture years differ by more than one year. Where either is missing, first registration years are compared instead.


Engine
Both engine sizes are recorded and differ by more than 100cc and by more than 10%.



A comparison that cannot be made counts as agreement. When at least two comparisons disagree, dvla_match is different: the VES record belongs to another vehicle, and none of its values (fuel, engine size, weight, CO2, Euro status, type approval, wheel plan) is used. dvla_evidence counts the disagreements.
Some make pairs are the same vehicle under another name: CHRYSLER-JEEP / JEEP, ROVER / AUSTIN, and motorhome converters such as FIAT / AUTO-TRAIL. They are found from the whole input file. A pair is an alias when it has at least 20 rows with comparable years (checks.dvla_alias_min_rows), and the years agree for at least 90% of them (checks.dvla_alias_min_year_agreement). This finds 392 pairs. The split is clear-cut:

Naming pairs agree on year 90–100% of the time.
Different makes, in pairs large enough to have qualified, agree 16.4% of the time. For example, BMW / AUDI agree 15.9% of the time.
Vehicles with the same make agree 99.90% of the time.




dvla_match

5.5 Plug-in hybrids: the DfT fuel detail
Neither source distinguishes a plug-in hybrid from any other hybrid. DVSA records Hybrid Electric (Clean) for a mild hybrid, a full hybrid and a plug-in alike, and Electric Diesel for both kinds of diesel hybrid; the VES fuel types map onto the same two labels. The DfT vehicle licensing statistics do distinguish them: table VEH0220, already read for the make/model naming scheme (Section 4.1), records eleven fuels, among them PLUG-IN HYBRID ELECTRIC (PETROL), PLUG-IN HYBRID ELECTRIC (DIESEL) and RANGE EXTENDED ELECTRIC.
VEH0220 counts vehicles rather than naming them, so the detail is attached by make and model (R/fuel_dft.R). Every DfT fuel and every harmonised fuel is put into the same set of narrow groups, and a vehicle is only ever matched against DfT rows in its own group:

The groups are what makes the replacement safe. A vehicle recorded as Electric can only match BATTERY ELECTRIC, so it can never become a hybrid; a petrol vehicle can only match PETROL, so it can never pick up a diesel fuel; and a petrol hybrid can only become one of the three petrol hybrid fuels. A range extender sits with the petrol hybrids, not with battery electric, because it has a petrol engine and DVSA records those vehicles as hybrids. Other and Steam have no DfT counterpart and are matched in no group at all.
Within its group a vehicle takes the most common DfT fuel for:

its DfT model string (fuel_DFT_src = dft_model), the value of dft_model from Section 4.3
its generic model (dft_genmodel), when the raw model text gave no DfT model string

A level is used only when one DfT fuel holds at least 0.9 of that level’s DfT vehicles in the group. Otherwise the vehicle is left unmatched and recorded as ambiguous_model or ambiguous_genmodel.
That threshold is the answer to models sold both as a plug-in and not. Model strings are nearly always clear-cut, because the string names the variant: “NIRO 3 PHEV S-A” against “NIRO 3 HEV S-A”, “X1 XDRIVE25E M SPORT AUTO” against “X1 SDRIVE 20I M SPORT MHEV A”, “XC40 + T4 RECHARGE AUTO” against “XC40 + B4 MHEV AUTO”. Of the DfT model strings that carry a petrol hybrid, 3,125 of 3,126 have one fuel above the threshold (measured once against the full build, as are the model shares below). Generic models often are not clear-cut: BMW X1 petrol hybrids are 56% mild hybrid and 44% plug-in, and KIA NIRO petrol hybrids 84% full hybrid and 16% plug-in, so an X1 or a NIRO whose model text gave no model string is left unmatched rather than guessed at. HYUNDAI KONA shows the other case: it is sold as petrol, battery electric and full hybrid but has never been sold as a plug-in, so its petrol hybrids are unambiguous at generic-model level and are matched.

What this does not do. The DfT fuel is a property of the make, model and variant, not of the individual vehicle, so a vehicle whose model text was matched to the wrong model string takes the wrong fuel with it. The match is only as good as Section 4, and model_confidence is the guide to that. Nor can it find a plug-in hybrid whose make/model DfT does not record at all (no_reference), or one of an ambiguous generic model: those vehicles are undercounted as ordinary hybrids, which makes 1,090,074 a lower bound on the plug-in fleet.

The recorded Euro status is standardised first (R/euro_status.R), because VES writes one status in many ways: “EURO 6 AP”, “EURO 6AP”, “EURO6AP” and “EURO 6 (AP)” all become “EURO 6 AP”. Case, spacing and punctuation are made consistent, “+” is written as PLUS, clear typing errors are fixed (V1 for VI, 1SC or 15C for ISC, 0BD for OBD), and repeats of the standard are dropped (“EURO 6 EURO 6 AP”, “EURO 5 (FIVE)”, “EURO VI E (6)”). Nothing else is removed, and euroStatus_DVLA keeps the value as supplied. The value is written as EURO, the standard, then the remaining letters and digits, with hyphens around the words TEMP, EVAP, ISC, FCM, BIS, OBD, WLTP and PLUS (“EURO 6 D-TEMP-EVAP-ISC”, “EURO VI OBD-E”). Spaces are kept only between two numbers (“EURO VI 66D0”, “EURO 5 134 2014”).
Each takes the first available of:

the recorded value (*_src = dvla or dvsa)
the most common value for the same make, model, birth year, fuel and engine size (variant). The engine size is the vehicle’s engine_cc from 5.4, so it may itself be backfilled, and electric vehicles match other electric vehicles at 0.
the most common value for the same make, model, birth year and fuel (model_year_fuel)
for euro_status only, the standard that was compulsory for new registrations when the vehicle was made (euro_schedule, Section 5.7)
otherwise missing (*_src empty)

For vehicles with a mismatched VES record, recorded VES values are ignored and filled as if missing. This affects the CO2 value of 115,761 vehicles.
A recorded CO2 of 0 g/km is only kept for a vehicle with no engine. Only a pure electric or fuel cell vehicle can emit nothing; anywhere else a zero is a value the VES never held, and taken at face value it would put millions of petrol cars and diesel vans in the “0 g/km” band. The zero is cleared in R/fuel_engine.R, before the backfill references are built, so that the modal CO2 of a variant is taken from real values only and a vehicle recorded as 0 is filled from similar vehicles instead. A vehicle with no fuel recorded is not known to be electric, so its zero goes too. co2Emissions_DVLA keeps the value as supplied, and co2_check records what happened:

5.7 Euro status from the registration date
A Euro status is recorded for only a minority of vehicles. The VES returns one mostly for vehicles first registered from 2018 onwards, so after the variant backfill of Section 5.6 44.6% of in-scope vehicles still had none.
The standards were phased in on fixed dates, though, and a vehicle cannot have been registered new in Great Britain after the date a standard became compulsory without meeting it. So where nothing else says otherwise, a missing Euro status takes the standard in force when the vehicle was made (R/euro_status.R, euro_status_src = euro_schedule).
Three decisions make that assumption as weak as the rules allow:

The compulsory dates, not the type-approval dates. Each standard opened for new type approvals a year or more before it became compulsory for all new registrations. Using the later date means a vehicle may well meet a newer standard than it is given here, but it cannot meet an older one.
The date the vehicle was made, not its British registration date. birth_date is the earliest of the DVSA first-used, registration and manufacture dates (Section 3.2), which for an import is the manufacture date rather than the later British first registration. Tested against the 11.3 million vehicles whose birth_date is more than a year before their first_use_date, birth_date errs towards an older standard and first_use_date towards a newer one, so birth_date is used (first_use_date only where birth_date is missing).

The percentages in the rest of this section were measured once, against the full build, by comparing the schedule with the vehicles that do have a recorded Euro status; they are a record of that check and are not recomputed here. - One schedule per vehicle class. Vans were a year or two behind cars, lorries and buses ran on the heavy-duty timetable, and motorcycles reached Euro 4 only in 2017. Applying the car dates to motorcycles would be too new for 99.98% of the motorcycles that do have a recorded status.

5.8 How “most common” is calculated
The pipeline builds these reference tables:

Only recorded values are counted, plus the 0 engine size given to vehicles with no engine. Backfilled values are never fed back into the tables.
Ties go to the lowest value (the smallest number, or alphabetically first for text), so results are the same on every run.
A group’s value is used only if at least backfill.min_vehicles vehicles had it recorded. The setting is 1.
Vehicles without a make, model or fuel contribute to no table and receive no backfilled values. Vehicles without a birth year are used only for the model-fuel table.



5.9 Assumptions and limitations

Two disagreements between DVSA and VES mean different vehicles. One disagreement is common for genuine matches: imports registered years after manufacture, and engine sizes recorded differently. A registration moved between two vehicles of the same make and year, where one engine size is missing, is not detected; the fuel check catches some of these.
DVSA fuel is trusted unless another record contradicts it. VES overrides it only for “Other”, and for Electric / Fuel Cells vehicles that VES shows as hybrids or as having an engine.
A recorded engine size on an Electric vehicle is evidence of an engine, unless VES confirms it is electric (for example a converted classic that keeps its original engine size on record), or the make/model is electric-only.
Vehicles with no engine have engine size 0. Range-extender and hybrid vehicles recorded as Electric by both DVSA and VES, with no engine size, get



Rare fuels are flagged, not corrected. LPG conversions, electric conversions of classic cars and uncommon factory variants are all legitimate, so only electric-only models, where the records disagree, are corrected.
The fuel check depends on the make/model cleaning. Merged or wrong models produce rare_for_model and implausible_for_model flags; these point to raw spellings worth reviewing. Small make/models (under 100 vehicles) are not checked, and on the 1% sample most make/models are no_reference.
A model’s DfT fuel is its vehicles’ fuel. The plug-in distinction of Section 5.5 is a property of the model string, not of the individual vehicle, so it is only as good as the make/model match and cannot find a plug-in hybrid of a model DfT records both ways. The plug-in counts are a lower bound.
A vehicle registered new after a standard became compulsory meets it. The Euro status of Section 5.7 is an assumption about the rules, not an observation of the vehicle. It is wrong for used imports and rebuilt vehicles, which take a British registration long after they were built; birth_date limits that, and euro_status_src separates assumed values from recorded ones so they can be dropped.
Vehicles of the same make, model, birth year and fuel share attributes. This is reasonable for wheel plan, type approval and test class. It is weaker for CO2 and weight, which vary with trim, gearbox and body style.
Birth year stands in for model year.
At the variant level, engine size must match to the cc. Near-identical engines (1596 cc vs 1598 cc) form separate groups; the model-year-fuel level then applies.
A vehicle with a backfilled engine size matches the most common variant of its make, model, year and fuel, and takes that variant’s attributes.
A single recorded vehicle is enough to fill a group. This follows from min_vehicles = 1.
Missing values are not random. VES values are mostly missing where no VES record was found, which is more common for older and scrapped vehicles. Their gaps are filled from vehicles that do have records.
“Other” is treated as one fuel group, although it covers a mix of fuels.
Euro status spellings are standardised, not interpreted (5.6). The letters after the standard are kept together, because the stage letter and the emission code cannot be told apart once the spacing varies: “EURO 6D AR” and “EURO 6 DAR” are both “EURO 6 DAR”, and stay separate from “EURO 6 AR”. Other misspellings still count as separate values. The derived euro_standard column (Section 6.1) is more robust.

For analysis sensitive to these assumptions, filter to recorded values with *_src IN ('dvsa', 'dvla'), or to fuel_check = 'ok'. The churn tables use the recorded DVSA fuel, engine size and test class columns by default.

6.1 Derived fields

euro_standard is the Euro emission standard number taken from the euro_status text, with Roman numerals converted. For example, “EURO 6 AP” gives 6 and “EURO VI E” gives 6. Heavy-duty (Roman) and light-duty (Arabic) standards share one scale, although they are different regulations.



6.2 Number plate decoding
The registration is upper-cased and stripped of non-alphanumeric characters (registration_clean). It is then matched against a sequence of plate formats, and the first match wins. The rules are an SQL translation of DVLAAPI::registration_analysis(), in the same order. The main formats are:









Format
Example
Issue period from
Location from




GB current (2001 onwards)
AB12CDE

Great Britain

“Great Britain or Northern Ireland”



Less common formats are also recognised: Q plates, diplomatic, Isle of Man, Republic of Ireland, French, Channel Islands, Gibraltar, Swiss, and strings that look like a VIN.

The plate period gives plate_date, plate_date_from (first day of the first month) and plate_date_to (first day of the last month).
vanity_plate is TRUE when birth_date falls outside the plate period, widened by 30 days (plates.vanity_tolerance_days) at each end.
vanity_plate is missing when the plate has no dated period, or the vehicle has no birth date.

Assumptions and limitations:

The DVSA registration is the plate the vehicle carries.
The rules are simple pattern checks. They follow the DVLAAPI package and should be read as indicative, not definitive.
vanity_plate flags any mismatch between plate and age, not only cherished plates:

imported vehicles registered years after manufacture
Q plates
re-registered vehicles
vehicles whose earliest date (often manufacture) is well before first registration

The period end is the first day of the last month, so the 30-day tolerance partly serves to cover the rest of that month.

title: Methodology
text:
7. Stage 5: Churn tables
Code: R/summary_churn.R · Outputs: outputs/tables/churn/ (file list in README_outputs.csv)
The churn tables describe how vehicles enter, move between and leave postcode areas. They reproduce the Sets 0–7 analysis of make_churn_output_tables_v2.R.
This section covers the method. outputs/reports/churn_tables_report.md documents the tables themselves for someone reading the CSVs without reading the code: table by table, which vehicles are counted, how each variable is grouped, what every column means, and how complete and how distributed each underlying variable is.

7.1 Population and definitions

Population: vehicles with test class 4 (cars, vans and small motorhomes), using the harmonised test_class (churn.test_class_column). Vehicles with a missing test class are excluded; the harmonised column leaves 0% of vehicles without one, against 13.6% for the anonymised test_class_ANON the churn v2 tables used, which is missing for every Northern Ireland vehicle. The Set 1 tables carry the class in a test_class column; churn v2 named it test_class_ANON.
Real PCA: any pca_YYYY value other than dead, unborn or unknown. NI (Northern Ireland) is a real PCA; churn.exclude_ni_rows removes it from table rows while still counting moves to and from it.
Status relative to a reference year:







Status
Meaning




dead
dead in the comparison year


unborn
unborn in the comparison year


same
same postcode area as the reference year


different
anything else, including a different area and unknown



Age is whole years at 1 June of the year: floor((1 June − first_use_date) in days / 365.25).
Bands (age, mileage, engine size) include their lower bound and exclude their upper bound. Engine 2000 cc is in “1700–2000”; 2001 cc is “>2000”.
Fuel groups:

fuel_simple, as in Section 6.1.
fuel3: Petrol, Diesel, Other.
An EV is Electric only. Electric Diesel is counted as a hybrid.




7.2 Movement measures

A move is a change of postcode area between two consecutive years in which both years hold a real PCA. A sequence such as LS → unknown → BD therefore counts no moves.
movement_rate is the number of moves between 2007 and 2017 divided by (age in 2017 − 3). It is only calculated for vehicles aged 4 or more in 2017.
movement_rate_window is the same number of moves divided by the number of consecutive-year pairs in which the vehicle was in a real PCA in both years.
movement_rate_2022 is the same as movement_rate for 2012–2022.
static_2017 means in the same real PCA in 2016, 2017 and 2018.
Per-vehicle history:

first_real_pca: the first real PCA seen from 2005.
birth_pca: the first real PCA immediately after an unborn year. It is missing for vehicles already alive in 2005.
ever_moved_pca: ever seen in a real PCA other than the first one.

Clean Air Zone category:

petrol_pre2006: petrol, first used before 2006, a proxy for pre-Euro 4.
diesel_pre2015: diesel, first used before 2015, a proxy for pre-Euro 6.
other: everything else.




7.3 Assumptions

(age − 3) is the time a vehicle has been observable. This assumes a first MOT at three years old. Northern Ireland tests at four, and early tests happen.
movement_rate understates movement for vehicles older than about 14. The numerator covers only the 11-year window, but the denominator keeps growing with age. movement_rate_window is the check for older vehicles.
different mixes two things: genuine moves and vehicles that became unobserved (unknown).
The CAZ categories use first use date, not the Euro status. Set 7 includes a cross-check of the proxy against the harmonised euro_status, which now covers 91.3% of in-scope vehicles against 14.5% with a VES value. Read that cross-check with care: since Section 5.7 fills a missing Euro status from the date the vehicle was made, most of the Euro statuses it compares are themselves derived from a date, so agreement is partly built in. euro_status_src on the enhanced table separates the recorded values, and churn.euro_column can be set to euroStatus_DVLA to check against recorded values only.
The data end in 2025, and 2025 is partial. 25,803,313 vehicles have a 2025 mileage against 36,734,471 in 2024, so a vehicle last seen in 2024 may simply not have been tested yet. Measures described as “left by” a year are measured against the last year in years.
The churn tables use the harmonised attributes by default (churn.test_class_column, churn.fuel_column, churn.engine_column, churn.euro_column), so they cover more vehicles than the values as supplied and carry the corrections of Section 5. Each setting takes the churn v2 column instead (test_class_ANON, fuel_DVSA, engineSize_DVSA, euroStatus_DVLA) to reproduce the old tables. What this changes, for class 4 vehicles:



Attribute
As supplied
Harmonised




Test class
86.4%
100%


Engine size
88.7%

Euro status

100%

The Set 7 Euro status check column is euro_status, named euro_status_recorded in churn v2, because the value may now be backfilled rather than recorded.
An engine size of 0 cc is its own band, 0 (electric). The harmonised engine_cc is 0 for the fuels with no engine, so the band is electric vehicles (1.66M class 4) and a handful of fuel cell vehicles. They are not small-engined vehicles, so the lowest size band starts at 1 cc and is named for that: 1-1400 in the 3 and 4 band breakdowns, 1-600 in the 100 cc breakdown and 1-1000 in the detailed one. Churn v2 treated 0 cc as missing. Set 3 gains an n_engine_zero column; n_engine_lt1400 keeps its name and now counts 1-1399 cc.
In churn v2 reproduction mode (engine_column: engineSize_DVSA) the same band instead holds every 0 cc recording, which is 48,800 diesel and 294 petrol vehicles as well as 11,550 electric ones.



7.4 The sets







Set
Contents




0
Where the first use date came from


1
Counts by PCA of each year’s status relative to 2017, and relative to 1, 2 or 3 years earlier (all ages, and aged 4+)


2
Vehicle counts by PCA × year by age, mileage, fuel and engine bands. Share of 2017 vehicles aged 4+ that stayed static 2016–2018, by characteristic and pairwise


3
Components of each PCA’s 2017 stock: a 3 × 3 cross-tab of 2016 status against 2018 status that sums to the total. Also mileage, age, fuel and engine counts, and the movement rate distribution


4
Electric vehicles by PCA: presence in 2017 and 2022, arrivals, departures, born here, high mileage


5
Mileage of vehicles that stayed, arrived or were new in 2016–2017


6
Mean movement rate by characteristic, and pairwise


7
CAZ categories by PCA and year, and vehicles present in 2018 but gone by 2023, by characteristic





7.5 Life path charts
Code: R/lifepath_alluvial.R · Outputs: outputs/figures/lifepath_alluvial/lifepath_alluvial_<PCA>.png
One alluvial chart per postcode area, ported from MOT-data-analysis/Rscripts/Churn/lifepath_alluvial.R. Each chart covers 2015-2019 (lifepath.years) and shows every vehicle in the area in at least one of those years, as long as it is not already dead in the first year or still unborn in the last.

A ribbon is one trajectory: a distinct sequence of states across the years, not one vehicle, and its width is the number of vehicles following it. Leeds has about 200 of them.
The states are the area itself, split into vehicles in it every year (stable) and in it in only some years (transient), any other postcode area, and the unborn, unknown and dead statuses of Section 3.3. Those statuses are what keep every year’s total the same, so nothing enters or leaves the chart.
Colour is the trajectory type: always in the area, there at the start and end, arriving (new or from elsewhere), leaving (scrapped or to elsewhere), or passing through. Flows that only carry a vehicle from unborn to unborn, or from dead to dead, are drawn faintly, because they are not movements.
Population: test class 4, using the harmonised test_class (lifepath.test_class_column). This setting is separate from the churn one so that the charts can cover Northern Ireland, whose vehicles have no anonymised test class at all.
Area names in the titles come from inputs/postcode_area_names.csv. The code XX gets no chart, as it is not a postcode area.

Assumptions:

“Scrapped” means the trajectory ends dead, which is the end of MOT testing and not necessarily scrapping (Section 3.3).
A vehicle counted as stable is stable only within the chart years. It may have moved before or after them.

title: Methodology
text:
8. Stage 6: Mileage summaries
Code: R/summary_mileage.R · Outputs: outputs/tables/mileage/
Method: for each year, every vehicle with a recorded mileage_YYYY contributes one row, and the rows are summed into:

total annual mileage, vehicle count and mean by PCA (or status), year and the Bristol legit_mileage flag
total mileage by legit flag and year
total mileage by test class and year, with class labels
total mileage by DVSA fuel and year

Each breakdown is written in long form and wide form (years as columns).
Area summaries for the mileage report (build_mileage_area_summaries(), target mileage_area_tables) hold sums and counts, so any grouping can be rebuilt from them:

mileage_by_pca_year_body_fuel.csv: by year, pca_YYYY value (postcode area or status), body type and fuel_simple: vehicles; vehicles with a mileage, with a mileage flagged plausible, and with a mileage Bristol removed; total and plausible mileage; negative and over-50,000 mileages; and the total and count of ages (the year minus the first use year), with negative ages counted apart.
mileage_by_age_year_body_fuel.csv: observed vehicles (a real PCA) by year, body type, fuel and age (capped at 40; -1 for a negative age), with their plausible mileage.
mileage_distribution_by_year_body.csv: recorded mileage in 1,000-mile bands up to 50,000, then wider bands, by year, body type and flag.

These feed outputs/reports/mileage_report.md (Section 9), which also uses postcode area boundaries (inputs/postcode_areas_100m.gpkg) and DfT small-area vehicle counts added up to postcode areas (inputs/dft_lsoa_vehicles_by_pca.csv); inputs/README.md describes how both were built.
Assumptions:

Mileage is annual as supplied. It is not rescaled or capped. Negative and very high values are included; the quality report counts them.
Bristol has already removed implausible mileage. Where legit_mileage_YYYY is FALSE, mileage_YYYY is empty. A recorded mileage either has the flag TRUE (plausible) or has no flag (not assessed; up to about 5% of recorded mileage a year, and more in a partial final year). The legit_mileage groups in the tables above are therefore TRUE and missing.
Vehicles are grouped by their status in that year. A vehicle recorded as unknown in a year that still has mileage appears under unknown.

Code: R/report_quality.R, R/report_inputs.R, R/reports.R, templates in reports/ · Outputs: outputs/quality/*.csv, outputs/quality/data_quality_report.md and the documents below

Row counts: input rows, vehicles in scope, and each combination of scope reasons.
Dates and duplicates: first-use date sources, and duplicated registrations.
PCA statuses: counts by year, plus sequence checks that should be zero:

vehicles dead and later seen in a PCA
vehicles seen in a PCA and later unborn

Make and model: vehicles by make and model method, the largest unmatched raw pairs, body type sources, and the comparison with DfT counts by year, body type, age and make/model (dft_stock_*.csv).
Number plates and VES: plate type mix, vanity rate, VES match rates, and (where the delivery supplies them) what changed between VES lookups.
DVSA–DVLA record match: dvla_match by number of disagreements, the VES values ignored as a result, and whether mismatched vehicles are the ones whose plate changed. The full list of suspected mismatches in the input file is suspected_dvla_mismatches.csv, with the make aliases used in dvla_make_aliases.csv.

title: Methodology
text:
10. Reproducibility

The whole pipeline is defined in _targets.R. It runs with targets::tar_make(), and only stages whose code, settings or inputs have changed are rebuilt. Editing a report template re-renders only that report.
All settings that change results are in config.yml.
The reference inputs are version-controlled in inputs/, with their source recorded in inputs/README.md.
Package versions are recorded in renv.lock.
Results are deterministic:

backfill and fuel ties are broken by value
make/model matching has no random element, and per-vehicle model choices break ties by candidate order
the sample project draws a 1% Bernoulli sample of input rows with seed 42

The make aliases are derived from the input, so a new Bristol delivery can change them slightly; they are written out for inspection.
vehicle_id depends on row order in the input file. Join to external data on registration_DVSA, not vehicle_id.

title: Methodology
text:
11. Validation
The unit tests run on every change. The other checks below were made once, when the pipeline was first built against the earlier annualised_with_ves.parquet delivery; their figures are a record of that validation and are not recomputed.

Unit tests (tests/testthat/) use small synthetic vehicles to check:

PCA status infill
the scope rule
date coalescing and duplicate flags
reading either Bristol delivery’s column names
make/model matching to the DfT names: each matching step, the vehicle-type check, derivatives, per-vehicle choices and the overrides file
DVSA–DVLA matching, with and without make aliases
the fuel rules: a mismatched VES record, hybrids recorded as Electric or Fuel Cells, fuel from engine size, corrections on an electric-only model, an LPG conversion, a removed engine size and a 0cc engine
backfill tie-breaking, minimum support and same-fuel matching
the Euro status schedule: the standard in force for each body type and date, that a recorded value is never overwritten, that a value too new for the vehicle is flagged, and that body types with no schedule stay missing
the DfT fuel detail: that no fuel group mixes two energy sources, that a model string settles a plug-in where the generic model cannot, that models DfT sells both ways are left alone, and that a plug-in match is refused for a vehicle with no engine size
band edges against R’s cut()
movement rates and PCA history
the Set 3 identity

The Euro status schedule and the DfT fuel detail were both profiled on the full input before being added. The schedule was compared with every vehicle that has a recorded Euro status, one body type at a time, and the choice of date, of schedule and of which body types to leave alone all come from that comparison (Section 5.7). The DfT fuel detail was checked for how often a model string and a generic model settle the plug-in question before the 0.9 threshold was set (Section 5.5).
DVSA–DVLA matching was profiled on the full input before choosing the rule. Year agreement was 99.95% for vehicles with the same make, 96–100% for naming pairs, and about 20% for genuinely different makes. Section 5.1 gives the current figures.
Plate decoding returned identical plate type, date and location to DVLAAPI::registration_analysis() for 40,038 registrations, and identical vanity flags.
Make/model cleaning was first a port of the legacy rules plus an AI lookup, audited in make_model_cleaning_audit.md. It has been replaced by the DfT naming in Section 4, whose comparison with DfT counts (Section 4.8) is rebuilt with every run.
Enhanced table against the legacy enhanced parquet on a 1% sample: for all 874,629 vehicles present in both, pca_YYYY in every year, plate type, date and location, the vanity flag and birth date were identical.
Churn tables on the same 1% sample: the legacy make_churn_output_tables_v2.R and this pipeline produced identical values in all 70 output files.
Full-data comparison (tests/compare_legacy.R) against the legacy enhanced parquet and churn v2 tables:

Every legacy vehicle is present. Of the 87,476,599 legacy vehicles, 87,464,875 matched a non-duplicated vehicle. The other 11,724 were also present but flagged dup_vrm, so the comparison left them out.
Matched vehicles agreed completely. For all 87,464,875, pca_YYYY in every year, plate type, date and location, the vanity flag and birth date were 100% identical.
The new table had 3,832,000 more vehicles, all from the wider scope rule. 3,747,116 of them qualified only through DVLA activity since 2005.
Churn tables differed only as the wider scope implies. Most cells differed by less than 1%. The largest absolute differences (about 55,000) were in the dead / unborn status counts of Sets 0 and 1, where the added vehicles fall. Large relative differences only occurred in cells that were near zero.

Every table

title: Data quality report
text:
Input rows: 138,238,617, covering 2005–2025.
Vehicles in scope (existed 2005 onwards): 93,352,241 (67.5% of input rows).
Rows sharing a registration with another row: 0.
VES records: 76.1% of input rows have one. Of in-scope vehicles with a VES record, 123,155 (0.17%) look like a different vehicle; they are listed in suspected_dvla_mismatches.csv.
PCA sequence checks: 0 vehicles recorded dead and later seen in a PCA, and 0 seen and later unborn. Both should be near zero.
Make and model: 94.9% of in-scope vehicles have a DfT generic model; 0.8% have a raw model that matched nothing, and 4.3% a placeholder such as UNKNOWN.
Against DfT counts (cars): in 2025, 33,298,028 cars were observed here against 38,490,385 licensed or SORN in the DfT statistics (86.5%); for cars first used three or more years earlier, 103.7%. Buses, HGVs and other vehicles are tested outside the MOT scheme, so few are here.
Fuel checks: 3,733 fuels corrected to Electric, and 55 fuels implausible for their make/model.
Plug-in hybrids: 94.5% of in-scope vehicles have a fuel_DFT from the DfT statistics, and 1,090,074 are plug-in hybrids or range-extended electrics, which neither DVSA nor DVLA distinguishes. 244,402 vehicles are of a make/model that DfT sells both as a plug-in and not, with nothing to say which this one is, so they keep their recorded fuel.
Euro status: 91.3% of in-scope vehicles have one, of which 33,468,440 come from the date the standard became compulsory. 10,332,946 vehicles carry a status naming a standard that did not exist when they were made; these are flagged in euro_check, not changed.
Mileage: 25,803,313 vehicles have a 2025 mileage, 70.2% of the 36,734,471 in 2024, so 2025 looks like a partial year.

title: Vehicles and mileage by postcode area
text:
Summary
Generated from reports/mileage_report.qmd by the MOT-pipline mileage_report target (profile: main). Edit the template, not this file.
This report describes the vehicles in the enhanced MOT table: how many there are, what kind, how far they are driven, how old they are and where they are, from 2005 to 2025. It compares the counts with DfT’s small-area licensing statistics, and ends with checks that point to possible problems in the data.
Definitions used throughout:
crumbs: Vehicles and mileage by postcode area

title: Vehicles and mileage by postcode area
text:
Vehicles observed in 2022: 45,018,795, of which 38,155,912 (84.8%) are cars. 39,474,199 (87.7%) have an annual mileage for the year.
Average annual mileage of cars: 6,619 miles in 2022, against 7,892 in



Average age of cars: 9.4 years in 2022, against 6.6 in



Years shown: charts over time cover 2005 to 2025. Maps and other single-year figures show 2022 at the latest: vehicles under three have not had their first MOT, so the fleet observed in the last 3 years of data is incomplete. Comparisons between selected years start in 2006, because the 2005 data looks lower quality (section 2). Mileage for 2025 is partial: fewer than 90% as many vehicles have one as in the year before.



observed: a vehicle is counted in a year when pca_YYYY is a postcode area (not unborn, dead or unknown): it was seen, usually at an MOT test, that year. Vehicles under three (four in Northern Ireland) have no MOT, so are largely missing.
annual mileage: Bristol’s mileage_YYYY. Averages use only mileage Bristol flagged as plausible (legit_mileage_YYYY is TRUE). Bristol has already removed the mileage it flagged as implausible, and a mileage with no flag was not assessed; section 6 counts both.
age: the year minus the year of first use.
body type: the DfT body type from make and model matching (methodology.md, Section 4.6). Other groups buses and coaches, heavy goods vehicles, other vehicles and vehicles with no body type.
fuel: the harmonised fuel grouped into Petrol, Diesel, Hybrid Electric, Electric and Other (fuel_simple).
postcode area: as recorded by Bristol. Northern Ireland is NI; XX has no boundary. Maps show Greater London enlarged in a box.
crumbs: Vehicles and mileage by postcode area

title: Vehicles and mileage by postcode area
text:
1. Where the data comes from

1.1 The chain of files
The mileage tables are the last step of a longer pipeline. Each step writes a file; the next step reads it. Nothing in the mileage step goes back to the original data.








Step
File
What it is




Input
annualised_with_ves_4.parquet
The vehicle-level annualised MOT table supplied to the project, one row per vehicle, with DVLA (VES) columns attached


Stage 1
outputs/intermediate/01_core.parquet
The input narrowed to the columns used, typed, with vehicles outside the scope removed


Stages 2-3
outputs/vehicles_enhanced.parquet
Cleaned make/model, harmonised fuel, engine size, body type and Euro status (93,352,241 vehicles)


Mileage
outputs/tables/mileage/*.csv
The 10 published tables that sections 2 to 5 describe


Mileage
outputs/quality/mileage_profile/*.csv
The measurements in this document



“Scope” means a vehicle is kept if it has any recorded mileage, or any recorded postcode area, or was born on or after 2005-01-01, or shows DVLA activity (tax, V5C, MOT expiry or first registration) since that date.
Bristol’s annualisation is taken as given. The pipeline does not re-derive annual mileage, the postcode area or the plausibility flag. mileage_YYYY is already annual miles, so no scaling is applied (mileage_scaling in section 1.3). How those columns are built belongs to Bristol’s documentation, not this one.


1.2 Which vehicles are counted
Unlike the churn tables, the mileage tables keep every MOT test class and every body type. Nothing is filtered out: a vehicle missing from a year is missing because it had no mileage or no postcode area that year, not because it was excluded.

Vehicles behind the mileage tables
Counted over the whole series: a vehicle counts under vehicles_with_mileage_in_any_year if it has a mileage in at least one year. The tables themselves are per vehicle-year, so these are upper bounds on what any single year holds.

vehicles_in_vehicles_enhanced: Every in-scope vehicle

vehicles_with_plausible_mileage_in_any_year: Has a mileage Bristol judged plausible in at least one year
vehicles_with_mileage_removed_in_any_year: Had a mileage judged implausible and removed in at least one year
vehicles_in_a_real_postcode_area_in_any_year: Was located in at least one year
vehicles_with_no_body_type: No DfT body type could be decided, so they fall in the Other group of the charts
vehicles_with_no_first_use_date: No age can be computed
vehicles_with_no_test_class: Missing from the test class tables

3. The vocabulary, pedantically
legit_mileage is Bristol’s judgement, and it has three states, not two. TRUE is a mileage it judged plausible. A blank is a mileage it did not assess. FALSE means it judged the mileage implausible and removed it, so a FALSE row never carries a mileage; n_mileage_removed counts those vehicles. Totals in this report are plausible mileage unless they say otherwise, and section 4.2 gives the size of the unassessed group year by year.
A postcode area is pca_YYYY: either a real area, or one of unborn (before the vehicle existed), dead (after its last MOT) or unknown (a year inside its life with no area recorded, which includes a new vehicle’s first years before its first MOT). “Observed” in this report means a real area.
body_type is the DfT body type attached in Stage 2, not the MOT test class, so it exists for vehicles with no test class.
The charts group it as Cars, Light goods vehicles, Motorcycles and Other, with everything else in Other.
fuel_simple is the harmonised fuel in six groups, which separates plug-in hybrids from other hybrids. fuel_DVSA is the fuel exactly as supplied, with every rare spelling, and is used only in the fuel tables.
Age is the year minus the year of first use. It can be negative, when a vehicle was observed before the date it was first used; those are counted separately rather than dropped (n_negative_age). The age table caps age at 40 and holds every negative age at -1.
Mileage bands in mileage_distribution_by_year_body.csv are named by their lower edge in miles: bands of 1,000 up to 50,000, then three wider bands, with negative mileage at -1000.

10. Comparison with DfT small-area counts
DfT publishes vehicle counts for small areas (LSOAs and their equivalents) in tables VEH0125 (all vehicles by body type, keepership and licence status), VEH0135 (ultra low emission vehicles) and VEH0145 (plug-in vehicles). data-raw/build_dft_lsoa_vehicles_by_pca.R takes these tables from the PlaceBasedCarbonCalculator build, where the counts DfT suppresses are reconstructed, and adds them up to postcode areas (inputs/dft_lsoa_vehicles_by_pca.csv). The tables give the first quarter of each year, so MOT year Y is compared with DfT counts at the end of March of Y + 1. DfT counts here are licensed and SORN vehicles together.
The two sources are not expected to agree exactly. DfT counts include vehicles under three, which have no MOT. DfT also places a vehicle at its keeper’s address, so company and lease cars are counted where the company is registered, while the MOT data places a vehicle where it was observed. The maps and tables below therefore compare each postcode area with the national ratio for 2022 (1.041 MOT cars per DfT car).



Figure 15: Vehicles observed in the MOT data for each vehicle in the DfT small-area counts (licensed and SORN).





Figure 16: Cars observed in the MOT data against the DfT count, relative to the national ratio. Blue: more cars in the MOT data than the national ratio suggests; red: fewer.





Figure 17: Share of DfT cars kept by a company. High shares mark areas where fleet and lease cars are registered.





Figure 18: Cars by postcode area in the two sources (log scales). The line is the national ratio; labelled areas differ from it by more than 25%.

12. Source files and how to rebuild
Every table this document describes is listed with its grain and contents in section 2.1, and every column of every one of them in section 2.2. Two further inputs are read directly by the charts and maps:

inputs/dft_lsoa_vehicles_by_pca.csv: DfT VEH0125, VEH0135 and VEH0145 by postcode area (data-raw/build_dft_lsoa_vehicles_by_pca.R).

The tables and this document are built by targets, so rebuilding only repeats what changed:
# the mileage tables, their measurements and this report
targets::tar_make(names = c("mileage_tables", "mileage_area_tables",
                            "mileage_profile_tables", "mileage_report"))

# just this document, from the tables already written
targets::tar_make(names = "mileage_report")
Editing reports/mileage_report.qmd re-renders this document only. Editing R/summary_mileage.R rebuilds the tables and then this document. Every number above is read from the files listed in section 2.1 and the measurements in outputs/quality/mileage_profile/, so nothing here can drift from the build it describes.

section: 13. Things to be careful about, in one place
text:
13. Things to be careful about, in one place







Issue
Detail




The last year is partial
2025 holds 25,803,313 vehicle-years with a recorded mileage against 36,734,471 in 2024, and 0.03% of that mileage was never assessed. Do not read a trend into the final year.


Young vehicles are missing from the recent years
A vehicle’s mileage is only known once it has had an MOT, at three years old, so the youngest ages empty out towards the end of the series, and the vehicles that do appear there are the ones tested unusually early. Section 11 quantifies it.


Unassessed mileage is not zero mileage
Bristol removed the mileage it judged implausible, so a recorded mileage is either plausible or unassessed. Treating the unassessed as zero would lose 8,170 vehicle-years in 2025 alone.


A growing share of the fleet has no location
The unknown group reaches 12,640,179 vehicles by 2025. They are in the vehicle counts and in no postcode area row, so the area rows do not sum to the fleet.


The mileage is Bristol’s, not ours
Annual mileage, the postcode area and the plausibility flag all come from Bristol’s annualisation and are taken as given. The pipeline applies no scaling and does not re-derive them.


Two different fuel columns
The test class and fuel tables use the columns as supplied (test_class_ANON, fuel_DVSA); the area tables use the harmonised body_type and fuel_simple. The same fleet therefore appears under two fuel schemes, and only the harmonised one separates plug-in hybrids.


Vehicles with no body type
2,878,353 vehicles (3.08%) have no DfT body type, all of them vehicles with no MOT test class. They are grouped as Other rather than dropped.


Vehicles with no age
123 vehicles (0%) have no first use date, so they appear in the vehicle and mileage tables but in no age table.


Vehicles with no test class
19,314,753 vehicles (20.69%) have no test class and are absent from the test class tables, which therefore total less than the fleet.


Negative and very large mileage
Over the whole series 0 vehicle-years carry a mileage below zero and 105,523 above 50,000. Both are left in the published tables and counted separately (n_negative_mileage, n_over_50k_mileage) rather than removed.


Negative ages are not all errors
n_negative_age in the area table counts every year before a vehicle was first used, so it is large by construction and is not a count of errors. Among vehicles actually observed in a postcode area, 248,649 have a first use date after the year they were seen in.


A mean has a changing denominator
A mean mileage is over the vehicles that have a recorded mileage, not over the fleet, and that denominator changes year by year. The tables carry counts and totals rather than means alone, so a mean can be recomputed over any chosen group.

1. What this document is for
Generated from reports/churn_tables_report.qmd by the MOT-pipline churn_tables_report target (profile: main). Edit the template, not this file: every number below is recomputed from the data each time the pipeline runs.
The churn tables answer the question “do vehicles stay in the same part of the country, and does that differ by age, mileage, fuel or engine size?” There are 71 CSV files in outputs/tables/churn/. This document explains, for each one:
No programming knowledge is assumed. Where a rule is fussy, the fussy version is given rather than a simplified one, because the simplified version is where mistakes come from. Column and file names appear like this.

title: Churn tables: what each one contains and exactly how it was made
text:
2. The short version

Every table is built from one intermediate file, outputs/intermediate/churn_base.parquet, which has one row per vehicle (79,741,922 vehicles) and one column per year for location and mileage.
A vehicle’s location in a year is a postcode area (“LS”, “BS”, “NI”), or one of three words standing in for “no location recorded”: unborn, dead, unknown.
Almost every table counts vehicles grouped by postcode area, and splits them either by year or by a characteristic (age, mileage, fuel, engine size, emissions category).
The biggest limitation is not missing data in the usual sense: it is that a vehicle is only located in years it had an MOT. In 2019, the best covered year, only 53.3% of vehicles had a known postcode area.
